Section I: The Regulatory Imperative: IRS Scrutiny and the Burden of Proof Under IRC Section 41

The federal research credit, codified at 26 U.S.C. § 41 (originally enacted in 1981 and made permanent by the Protecting Americans from Tax Hikes (PATH) Act of 2015, enacted as Division Q of Public Law 114-113), provides a dollar-for-dollar reduction in federal income tax liability designed to encourage domestic research investment. Under 26 U.S.C. § 41(a)(1), the regular research credit equals 20% of the excess of a taxpayer's qualified research expenses (QREs) for the taxable year over a statutory base amount. Under 26 U.S.C. § 41(c)(4), the Alternative Simplified Credit (ASC), reported in Section B of IRS Form 6765, equals 14% of the amount by which current-year QREs exceed 50% of the taxpayer's average QREs for the three preceding taxable years, or 6% of current-year QREs if the taxpayer had no QREs in any one of those three preceding taxable years. Because the credit directly reduces tax liability, and because qualified small businesses may elect under 26 U.S.C. § 41(h) to apply up to $500,000 per year of the credit against the employer's share of payroll taxes, the Internal Revenue Service subjects IRC § 41 claims to stringent technical and financial examination.
1.1 Dissecting the Statutory and Regulatory Four-Part Test

To qualify for the research credit, activities must relate to the development or improvement of a business component, must be conducted within the United States, the Commonwealth of Puerto Rico, or a U.S. possession (the foreign-research exclusion appears at 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(4)(F)), and must satisfy all four requirements of 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(2), commonly known as the Four-Part Test.

items: The Section 174A / Section 174 Permitted Expenditure and Technical Uncertainty Test (26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1)(A); Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(2)(i), (a)(3)(i)): The research must involve expenditures eligible to be treated as domestic research or experimental expenditures under 26 U.S.C. § 174A (for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2024, following enactment of Public Law 119-21, commonly called the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, on July 4, 2025), or as specified research or experimental expenditures under 26 U.S.C. § 174 for earlier periods. Under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(3)(i), research is undertaken for the purpose of discovering information only if it is intended to eliminate uncertainty concerning the capability or method for developing or improving a business component, or the appropriate design of that business component, where the information available to the taxpayer at the outset does not establish that capability, method, or design.

The Discovering Technological Information Test (26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1)(B)(i); Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(4)): The research must be undertaken for the purpose of discovering information that is technological in nature. Under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(4), information is technological in nature if the process of experimentation used to discover it fundamentally relies on principles of the physical or biological sciences, engineering, or computer science. A taxpayer may employ existing technologies and rely on existing principles of those sciences to satisfy this requirement.

The Business Component Test (26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1)(B)(ii), (d)(2); Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(2)(ii)): The taxpayer must intend to apply the discovered information in developing a new or improved business component, defined under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(2)(B) as any product, process, computer software, technique, formula, or invention that is to be held for sale, lease, or license, or used by the taxpayer in its trade or business. Under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(2)(A), the Four-Part Test is applied separately to each business component, and under § 41(d)(2)(C), any plant process, machinery, or technique for commercial production of a business component is treated as a separate business component from the product being produced.

The Process of Experimentation Test for a Qualified Purpose (26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1)(C), (d)(3); Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(5)–(6)): Under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(6), the "substantially all" requirement is satisfied only if 80% or more of a taxpayer's research activities with respect to the business component, measured on a cost or other consistently applied reasonable basis (and without regard to the separate wage rule of § 1.41-2(d)(2)), constitute elements of a process of experimentation for a qualified purpose. Under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(5)(i), a process of experimentation is a process designed to evaluate one or more alternatives to achieve a result where the capability, method, or appropriate design of that result is uncertain at the beginning of the research activities, and it may involve modeling, simulation, or a systematic trial-and-error methodology. Under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(3) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(5)(ii), a qualified purpose relates to a new or improved function, performance, reliability, or quality of the business component, and research relating to style, taste, cosmetic, or seasonal design factors does not qualify. In addition, the statutory exclusions in 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(4)(A)–(H) bar research after the beginning of commercial production, adaptation of an existing business component to a particular customer's requirement, duplication of an existing business component, surveys and management studies, internal-use software (unless it satisfies the high-threshold-of-innovation test or another exception under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(c)(6)), foreign research, research in the social sciences, arts, or humanities, and funded research.

body.text: In Siemer Milling Co. v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2019-37, 117 T.C.M. (CCH) 1196 (filed April 15, 2019, Judge Buch), the U.S. Tax Court sustained the IRS's disallowance of 100% of the taxpayer's claimed research credits across all seven projects for its tax years ended May 31, 2011 ($122,424) and May 31, 2012 ($116,246), totaling $238,670 (several secondary summaries round this to "over $235,000"). Siemer Milling, an Illinois-based wheat flour miller whose credit studies had been prepared since 2004 by its outside accounting firm, CliftonLarsonAllen, claimed credits for projects including flour heat treatment, implementation of Pulsewave milling technology, testing of wheat hybrids, and ozone integration. The Tax Court held that the taxpayer failed to show that it formulated and tested hypotheses, evaluated alternatives, or engaged in modeling, simulation, or systematic trial and error, and it also disallowed several projects under the technological-in-nature test. Drawing repeatedly on Union Carbide Corp. & Subs. v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2009-50, aff'd, 697 F.3d 104 (2d Cir. 2012), the Tax Court in Siemer Milling described a qualifying process of experimentation as one that must involve a methodical plan with a series of trials to test a hypothesis, analyze the data, refine the hypothesis, and retest it, so that the work constitutes experimentation in the scientific sense. Because Siemer Milling did not produce documentation demonstrating that it formulated and tested scientific hypotheses or identified the principles of engineering or the physical or biological sciences on which it relied, the court sustained the IRS's disallowance in full.
1.2 The New Era of Disclosure, Form 6765 Section G, and Documentation Mandates

Heightened IRS enforcement has shifted substantiation from a reactive audit-defense task to an up-front filing requirement. Under Treas. Reg. § 301.6402-2(b)(1), any claim for refund or credit "must set forth in detail each ground upon which a credit or refund is claimed and facts sufficient to apprise the Commissioner of the exact basis thereof." The IRS has litigated this "specificity requirement" in research credit refund cases. In Harper v. United States, 847 F. App'x 408 (9th Cir. 2021) (No. 19-55933, decided February 25, 2021), the government argued that amended returns attaching Form 6765 lacked sufficient specificity; the Ninth Circuit reversed the district court's dismissal, holding that the IRS had waived the specificity requirement by substantively examining the claims. In Premier Tech, Inc. v. United States, No. 2:20-cv-890 (D. Utah), and Intermountain Electronics, Inc. v. United States, No. 2:20-cv-00501 (D. Utah), the government likewise argued that a refund claim supported only by an attached Form 6765 failed the specificity requirement. Following IRS News Release IR-2021-203 (October 15, 2021) and Chief Counsel memorandum FAA 20214101F, research credit refund claims filed on or after January 10, 2022 had to include specified information. After the IRS's June 18, 2024 update (announced in FAQ 21 on the IRS page "IRS sets forth required information for a valid research credit claim for refund"), taxpayers filing amended returns or refund claims that include an IRC § 41 credit must provide three core items of information when the claim is filed:

items: Identification of all business components to which the Section 41 research credit claim relates for that year.
For each business component, a description of all research activities performed.
The total qualified employee wage expenses, total qualified supply expenses, and total qualified contract research expenses for the claim year (which a properly completed Form 6765 satisfies).

body.text: Effective for claims postmarked on or after June 18, 2024, the IRS waived the requirement to include two additional items, the names of the individuals who performed each research activity and the information each individual sought to discover, at the time of filing, although examiners may still request both items if the claim is selected for examination. The IRS also provided a transition period during which a timely but deficient claim could be "perfected" within 45 days after the IRS issued Letter 6428; that transition period was extended three times and ended on January 10, 2026. For claims filed after that date, a refund claim that omits the three required items is subject to rejection without the transition-period opportunity to perfect, which makes complete, component-level information at the time of filing essential.

For original and amended returns alike, the IRS has institutionalized project-level cost reporting through its redesign of Form 6765, Credit for Increasing Research Activities, first used for 2024 tax years, and the accompanying Instructions for Form 6765 (Rev. December 2025), which state that they are for use with the January 2025 revision of the form. The redesigned form includes Section E (Other Information, lines 37–41), which must be completed whenever QREs are reported on line 48; Section F (Qualified Research Expenses Summary, lines 42–48); and Section G (Business Component Information, columns 49(a)–(f) and lines 50–56). When Section G applies, taxpayers complete it before Section F and report business components in descending order of QREs until the reported components account for at least 80% of total QREs, subject to a maximum of 50 business components; any remaining components are reported together as "Aggregate Business Components" in column 49(c). Columns 49(a)–(e) capture the controlled-group member's employer identification number (EIN), the principal business activity code, the business component's name or unique identifier, the business component type ("Product," "Process," or other), and, where applicable, the software type (internal use software, dual function software, or software excepted from internal-use treatment). Column 49(f) calls for additional information, and under the current instructions it is required only on amended returns and administrative adjustment requests that claim a credit not claimed on the original return or that increase the credit; it is not required on timely filed original returns. Lines 50–56 require a component-level disaggregation of QREs, separating in-house wages into wages for direct conduct of research (line 50), direct supervision (line 51), and direct support (line 52), totaled on line 53, followed by supplies (line 54), rental or lease costs of computers (line 55), and contract research expenses (line 56).

To keep the analysis current: under the Instructions for Form 6765 (Rev. December 2025), Section G is optional for all filers for tax years beginning before 2026, and it is required for tax years beginning after 2025, subject to two exceptions. Section G is not required for (1) a qualified small business under § 41(h)(3) that checks the box to elect the reduced payroll tax credit, or (2) a taxpayer whose total QREs on line 48 (on a controlled-group basis) are $1.5 million or less and whose average annual gross receipts for the prior three tax years are $50 million or less, when the credit is reported on an original return.
1.3 IRS Audit Procedures, Recordkeeping Rules, and the Qualitative Documentation Gap

Under 26 U.S.C. § 6001, Treas. Reg. § 1.6001-1, and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(d), a taxpayer claiming the research credit must retain records in sufficiently usable form and detail to substantiate that the expenditures claimed are eligible for the credit. The substantiation and recordkeeping chapter of the IRS Audit Techniques Guide: Credit for Increasing Research Activities (i.e. Research Tax Credit) IRC § 41 instructs examiners that failure to maintain required records is an independent basis for disallowing the credit, and it describes the use of a formal notice of inadequate records under Treas. Reg. § 1.6001-1(d).

The RCCATG describes the procedures that a well-constructed research credit study should include, such as review of primary accounting records, gathering corroborating technical evidence, physical inspection of some operations, and interviews with employees, and it directs examiners to evaluate whether a study actually performed those procedures and whether the taxpayer established a direct nexus linking accounting expenditures (W-2 wages, supply invoices, contractor payments) to specific qualified business components. Nexus is discussed in the RCCATG as a central weakness of many research credit claims. Examiners are directed to weigh oral testimony carefully, considering whether the witnesses actually performed the research and how much time has passed.

The IRS guidance establishes two administrative doctrines that expose superficial or automated claims to disallowance. First, regarding strict limits on estimation, the IRS is not required to accept estimates of qualified research expenses when actual documentation exists. Under the Audit Techniques Guide's synthesis of judicial precedent, courts permit estimation only if the taxpayer lacks contemporaneous records, first proves that it actually engaged in qualified research under IRC § 41(d), shows that the absence of records is not an "inexactitude" of its own making, and shows that the only remaining issue is quantifying the dollar amount. In Little Sandy Coal Co. v. Commissioner, 62 F.4th 287 (7th Cir. 2023) (decided March 7, 2023), affirming T.C. Memo. 2021-15, the Seventh Circuit affirmed the disallowance of a shipbuilder's research credit for its tax year ended June 2014 because the taxpayer failed to prove that substantially all (80% or more) of its research activities on the vessels at issue were elements of a process of experimentation. The court found that the taxpayer offered arbitrary allocations rather than a principled way to measure experimentation-related activity, cautioning that shortcut estimates will not suffice, and it noted that the taxpayer's "all or nothing" approach of claiming entire vessels, rather than identifiable subcomponents, prevented the courts from applying the shrinking-back rule. At the same time, the Seventh Circuit agreed with the taxpayer that direct support and direct supervision activities belong in both the numerator and the denominator of the "substantially all" fraction. The Tax Court had also sustained the IRS's deficiency and a 20% accuracy-related penalty, and the Seventh Circuit affirmed the Tax Court's decision.

In the primary text of the IRS Audit Techniques Guide's discussion of prepackaged submissions, the IRS warns examiners that taxpayers and study providers increasingly submit voluminous "prepackaged material" describing their methodology, which on review often fails to substantiate that the taxpayer actually paid or incurred QREs as claimed and contains information that is not germane to the audit. Accordingly, the RCCATG directs examiners to issue an Information Document Request (IDR) for a copy of the study provider's engagement letter together with the mandatory research credit claim IDR (Exhibit C), to consider a summons if the taxpayer refuses, and to request any supplemental contracts. The RCCATG flags contingent fees as a factor to consider, noting that when the fee depends on the final claim amount, some fee agreements shift control over resolution of the issue to the preparer, and it uses the engagement letter to help determine whether a reportable transaction exists under Treas. Reg. § 1.6011-4 (with related Form 8886 disclosure and 26 U.S.C. § 6707A penalties).
Section II: Analysis of Integrated R&D Services: Pilot.com R&D Tax Credit Reviews
2.1 Pilot.com's Value Proposition, Payroll Tax Offset Mechanics, and Workflow

Pilot (pilot.com) is a San Francisco-based startup and small-business accounting firm founded in 2017 that describes itself as "the largest startup and small business accounting firm in the US" and offers bookkeeping, tax preparation, fractional CFO services, and R&D tax credit preparation. Third-party trackers report total funding between roughly $158 million and $222 million (Pilot itself announced a $60 million Series C led by Sequoia Capital in January 2021, bringing its total to $120 million at that time, followed by a Series C extension in March 2021 at a reported $1.2 billion valuation), and published headcount estimates range from about 300 to about 416 employees. These figures are therefore reported here as third-party estimates rather than verified facts. According to Pilot's pricing page as reviewed for this edition, Pilot's bookkeeping plans include Essentials at $99 per month (for up to $100,000 in monthly expenses), a Core plan, and a Custom plan priced through sales. Pilot's corporate income tax preparation starts at $1,000+ per year for single-member LLCs, $2,000+ per year for partnerships and S corporations, and $2,450+ per year for C corporations, each billed annually, and each tax plan must be purchased together with Pilot Bookkeeping. Pilot's fractional CFO services start at $1,750, $3,150, and $5,250 per month for its Basic, Essentials, and Custom tiers, respectively.

Pilot's primary R&D credit value proposition targets pre-profit startups electing the Qualified Small Business (QSB) payroll tax credit under 26 U.S.C. § 41(h) and 26 U.S.C. § 3111(f). Under § 41(h)(3)(A), a corporation, partnership, or individual business (excluding organizations exempt from tax under § 501, and aggregating controlled groups under § 41(f)(1)) is a QSB for a taxable year only if (1) its gross receipts for that taxable year are less than $5,000,000, and (2) it had no gross receipts for any taxable year preceding the five-taxable-year period ending with that taxable year. For example, for a calendar-year 2026 claim, the five-year window spans 2022 through 2026, so any gross receipts in 2021 or earlier disqualify the business from the payroll election. In addition, under § 41(h)(4)(B)(ii), a taxpayer may not make the payroll election for a taxable year if it has made the election for five or more preceding taxable years, which effectively limits the election to five taxable years.

For taxable years beginning after December 31, 2022, Section 13902 of the Inflation Reduction Act of 2022 (Public Law 117-169) increased the maximum annual payroll tax credit election from $250,000 to $500,000 by adding a second $250,000 tranche that may be applied against the employer's share of Medicare tax. Claiming the payroll credit involves three linked IRS filings. First, on IRS Form 6765, Section D (lines 33a–36), the QSB makes the election by checking line 33a and entering on line 34 the portion of the research credit (up to $500,000) to be applied against payroll taxes. Under § 41(h)(4)(A), the election must be made on or before the due date (including extensions) of the original income tax return; Pilot's R&D page likewise states that the PATH Act payroll credit cannot be taken on an amended return. By contrast, the income tax credit under § 41(a) may generally be claimed on an amended return within the refund limitations period of 26 U.S.C. § 6511(a). Second, IRS Form 8974, Qualified Small Business Payroll Tax Credit for Increasing Research Activities, computes the amount of the credit usable in each quarter. The credit may first be claimed for the first calendar quarter beginning after the income tax return containing the election is filed. Per the Instructions for Form 8974 (Rev. December 2024), starting with the first quarter of 2023 the credit is first used to reduce the employer share of Social Security tax (§ 3111(a)) up to $250,000 per quarter, any remaining credit reduces the employer share of Medicare tax (§ 3111(b)) for the quarter, and any excess is carried forward to the next quarter. Third, Form 8974 is attached to IRS Form 941, Employer's Quarterly Federal Tax Return (or Form 943 or 944 for annual filers), where the credit reduces the employer's payroll tax liability. Pilot states that it works with payroll providers to apply the credit and that it has a partnership with Gusto that applies the credit automatically.

Pilot's blog cautions clients that self-serve questionnaires "make the customer do all the work," warns that the R&D credit is a frequent target of scams, recommends asking any provider for a sample report, and describes a three-step workflow:

items: Step 1 (Interview): Pilot's team holds a call with the client to learn about the business and its research and to identify what may qualify. Pilot presents this as more thorough than self-serve questionnaires. (Pilot's main R&D product page does not itself mention an interview step; the interview is described in Pilot's blog article on how its R&D credit service works.)

Step 2 (R&D Study report): Pilot describes the R&D Study report as its core deliverable, intended to support the claim in an audit. According to Pilot, the report covers the company and its activities, eligible expenses with supporting documents, and a technical explanation of how the research meets each part of the IRS Four-Part Test. Pilot states that its team combines tax expertise with technical backgrounds; it does not identify specific engineering credentials.

Step 3 (Tax forms and audit support): Pilot completes the credit forms (Forms 6765, 8974, and 941) based on the report. With Pilot Tax, Pilot files on the client's behalf; otherwise, it coordinates with the client's tax preparer. Pilot states that it will help clients defend their claims if audited, though its product page gives no detail on the scope of that support. Pilot's blog also states that "100% of our clients who have applied for payroll offsets have received their money"; this is a vendor statement that could not be independently verified.

body.text: 2.2 Analysis of Pilot.com Reviews, Pricing, and the Limits of Financial Aggregation

First, a review of customer ratings on major review aggregators shows a divergence between Pilot.com's core competency (startup bookkeeping and finance operations) and specialized R&D tax engineering. On G2, Pilot holds an overall rating of 4.7 out of 5.0 stars across 143 reviews, and G2 lists Pilot's offerings as bookkeeping, fractional CFO, and tax services. On Trustpilot, Pilot.com holds a TrustScore of 2.9 out of 5.0 ("Average") across 20 reviews, six of them in the past 12 months, with a distribution of 65% 5-star, 0% 4-star, 0% 3-star, 5% 2-star, and 30% 1-star. None of the 20 Trustpilot reviews mentions R&D tax credits. Of particular relevance to tax compliance, three 1-star Trustpilot reviews concern Pilot's tax services: an April 2026 reviewer reports paying nearly $2,400 for a tax engagement that amounted only to an extension filing, with poor support; a January 2026 reviewer describes the tax service as priced well above average, criticizes communication, and alleges that the firm failed to mention cost-saving options while focusing on upselling; and a November 2024 reviewer complains that tax-related emails continued after the company had closed.

Pilot charges a fee of 20% of the total R&D tax credit received. Pilot's own calculator illustrates a $6,000 fee on a $30,000 credit; applying the same percentage, the fee would be $20,000 on a $100,000 credit and $100,000 on a credit equal to the $500,000 maximum annual payroll election. Pilot's pricing and R&D pages do not mention a flat-fee alternative.

Beyond direct cost, the pricing distinction carries regulatory weight during an IRS examination. As noted in Section 1.3, the RCCATG directs examiners to request the study provider's engagement letter and flags contingent fees as a consideration because fee arrangements tied to the final claim amount can shift control over resolution of the issue and may bear on whether a reportable transaction with contractual protection exists under Treas. Reg. § 1.6011-4 (triggering Form 8886 disclosure and 26 U.S.C. § 6707A penalties). Section 10.35 originally contained the "covered opinion" rules referenced in the 2008 RCCATG, but Treasury withdrew those rules in final regulations issued in June 2014 and replaced § 10.35 with a general competence standard. The Circular 230 provision that governs contingent fees is § 10.27 (31 C.F.R. § 10.27), which generally prohibits a practitioner from charging a contingent fee for services rendered in connection with any matter before the IRS, including the preparation of an original return, subject to limited exceptions (for example, services in connection with an IRS examination of or challenge to an original return, or to an amended return or refund claim filed within 120 days after the taxpayer receives written notice of the examination or challenge; certain claims relating solely to statutory interest or penalties; and judicial proceedings). In Ridgely v. Lew, 55 F. Supp. 3d 89 (D.D.C. 2014), the court held that the IRS lacks statutory authority to enforce § 10.27's contingent-fee restrictions with respect to the preparation and filing of ordinary refund claims, and the IRS did not appeal. Whether a particular percentage-of-credit arrangement implicates § 10.27 therefore depends on the provider's status as a Circular 230 practitioner, the services performed, and whether the claim is made on an original return or on an ordinary refund claim. This edition does not conclude that any provider's fee arrangement violates Circular 230; it notes only that percentage-based fees draw examiner attention under the RCCATG.
Under 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(1)–(3) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(b)–(e), QREs fall into four statutory categories:

items: Employee Wages for Qualified Services (26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2)(A)(i), (B), (D); Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(c)–(d)): Wages as defined in 26 U.S.C. § 3401(a) (excluding wages taken into account for the § 51(a) Work Opportunity Credit) paid for (i) engaging in the actual conduct of qualified research, (ii) the direct supervision of qualified research, meaning the immediate supervision (first-line management) of that research and not higher-level management, or (iii) the direct support of qualified research, meaning services in direct support of persons conducting or directly supervising the research (for example, a machinist building an experimental model or a clerk compiling research data), but not general administrative services such as payroll, accounting, or janitorial work.

Supplies Used in the Conduct of Qualified Research (26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2)(A)(ii), (C); Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(b)(1)–(2)): Tangible property used and consumed in the conduct of qualified research, excluding land and improvements to land, property subject to depreciation, and general and administrative expenses such as ordinary utilities. Under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(b)(2)(ii), additional extraordinary utility expenditures may be treated as supplies to the extent the taxpayer establishes that the special character of the research required them.

Computer Rental or Lease Costs (26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2)(A)(iii); Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(b)(4)): Amounts paid or incurred to another person for the right to use (time-share) computers in the conduct of qualified research, such as cloud computing environments used for development and testing, provided the computer is owned and operated by someone other than the taxpayer, is located off the taxpayer's premises, and the taxpayer is not the primary user.

Contract Research Expenses (26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(3); Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(e)): Generally 65% of amounts paid or incurred to a person other than an employee for qualified research performed on the taxpayer's behalf. Under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(e)(2), the research is performed on the taxpayer's behalf only if the agreement is entered into before the research is performed and, among other conditions, requires the taxpayer to bear the expense even if the research is not successful (§ 1.41-2(e)(2)(iii)). The percentage increases to 75% for amounts paid to a qualified research consortium under § 41(b)(3)(C) and to 100% for amounts paid to eligible small businesses, universities, and federal laboratories for qualified energy research under § 41(b)(3)(D).

body.text: While accounting software can readily aggregate W-2 payroll totals, vendor payments, and cloud hosting invoices (the what and how much), general ledger categories do not record why an architecture failed, which hypotheses were tested, or what share of a cloud server cluster was used for experimental load testing rather than for commercial production hosting, which is excluded as research after the beginning of commercial production under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(4)(A).
Section III: Justification for Specialized Consultancy: Compliance Rigor and Legislative Agility
3.1 Dedicated Focus, the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (IRC Section 174A), and Failed Project Rules

This legislative complexity is most acute in the interplay among the IRC § 41 research credit, IRC § 280C(c), Form 6765 Section G, and the capitalization or deduction of research or experimental expenditures under IRC § 174 and § 174A.

headers: Prior / Legacy Regime and Effective Period
Current Controlling Regime and Effective Date
Key Thresholds, Elections, and Transition Deadlines

cells: Domestic research or experimental expenditures (IRC § 174 vs. IRC § 174A)

Tax years beginning in 2022–2024 (TCJA, Pub. L. 115-97, § 13206(a)): Mandatory capitalization and 5-year ratable amortization (using a midpoint convention); software development treated as research or experimental expenditure.

Tax years beginning after December 31, 2024 (Pub. L. 119-21, § 70302(a), enacted July 4, 2025): New 26 U.S.C. § 174A permits a current deduction of domestic research or experimental expenditures under § 174A(a), or an elective amortization over not less than 60 months under § 174A(c).

Small business retroactive election (Rev. Proc. 2025-28): Eligible small businesses meeting the § 448(c) gross receipts test (a $31 million average for 2025) could elect to apply § 174A retroactively to tax years beginning after December 31, 2021. Elections made on amended returns or administrative adjustment requests were due by the earlier of July 6, 2026 or the § 6511 refund deadline for each year; that window has now closed. Separately, all taxpayers may elect to deduct unamortized 2022–2024 domestic balances in full in the first tax year beginning after December 31, 2024, or ratably over that year and the next.
Foreign research or experimental expenditures (IRC § 174)
Tax years beginning in 2022–2024 (TCJA): Mandatory capitalization and 15-year ratable amortization from the midpoint of the year paid or incurred.
Tax years beginning after December 31, 2024 (Pub. L. 119-21, § 70302(b)): Amended 26 U.S.C. § 174 applies only to foreign research and retains mandatory 15-year amortization.
Under amended 26 U.S.C. § 174(d), for foreign research property disposed of, retired, or abandoned after May 12, 2025, no immediate recovery is allowed and the 15-year amortization continues.
Section 280C(c) credit-deduction coordination
Tax years beginning in 2022–2024 (TCJA rule): The capitalized research expenditure amount was reduced only to the extent the § 41 credit exceeded the current-year amortization deduction.

Tax years beginning after December 31, 2024 (Pub. L. 119-21): Under 26 U.S.C. § 280C(c)(1), the amount of domestic research expenditures otherwise taken into account under § 174A is reduced by the full amount of the § 41(a) credit, unless the taxpayer elects the reduced credit under § 280C(c)(2).

The reduced-credit election is made on Form 6765, Item A, on a timely filed original return; it cannot be made or changed on an amended return and is irrevocable once made. Electing reduces the regular credit to 15.8% (line 13) or multiplies the ASC by 79% (line 26). Rev. Proc. 2025-28 allowed eligible small businesses to make a late § 280C(c)(2) election, or revoke a prior one, for 2022–2024 by the earlier of July 6, 2026 or the § 6511 deadline; that window has also closed.
QSB payroll tax credit (IRC § 41(h) and § 3111(f))
Tax years beginning before January 1, 2023 (PATH Act): Maximum $250,000 per year payroll tax credit, usable only against the employer share of Social Security tax (§ 3111(a)).

Tax years beginning after December 31, 2022 (Inflation Reduction Act, Pub. L. 117-169, § 13902): Maximum $500,000 per year; the credit first reduces the employer share of Social Security tax (up to $250,000 per quarter under the Form 8974 instructions) and then the employer share of Medicare tax under § 3111(b), with any excess carried forward.

Requires current-year gross receipts under $5,000,000, no gross receipts before the five-taxable-year period ending with the credit year, and no more than five taxable years of elections; the election is made on Form 6765, Section D (lines 33a and 34), on a timely filed original return.
Form 6765 Section G business component disclosure
Tax years beginning before 2026: Completing Section G (columns 49(a)–(f) and lines 50–56) is optional for all filers.

Tax years beginning after 2025 (Instructions for Form 6765, Rev. December 2025): Section G is required and is completed before Section F, covering at least 80% of QREs across no more than 50 business components, with the remainder aggregated.

Exceptions: (1) a QSB electing the Section D payroll tax credit; or (2) a taxpayer with QREs of $1.5 million or less and average annual gross receipts for the prior three years of $50 million or less, reporting the credit on an original return. Column 49(f) is required only on amended returns and administrative adjustment requests that claim a new or increased credit.

body.text: As this statutory architecture demonstrates, the enactment of Public Law 119-21 (enacted July 4, 2025) fundamentally altered the economics of the IRC § 41 credit by restoring immediate domestic expensing under 26 U.S.C. § 174A for tax years beginning after December 31, 2024. For 2022–2024, the special window that allowed eligible small businesses to reopen those years under Revenue Procedure 2025-28 closed on July 6, 2026 (or earlier for any year whose § 6511 refund deadline fell first; for many calendar-year taxpayers, the 2022 refund window closed in April 2026). Taxpayers that missed the window generally continue to recover remaining 2022–2024 domestic balances under the transition rules for unamortized amounts. Because full expensing under § 174A also triggers the § 280C(c)(1) reduction for the full amount of the credit unless the reduced-credit election under § 280C(c)(2) is made on a timely original return, and because that election is irrevocable, navigating these interdependent elections calls for careful modeling rather than static tax-software defaults.

Under United States federal tax law, the eligibility of failed or abandoned R&D projects is governed by Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(3)(ii), which establishes a broader, taxpayer-favorable standard in two respects. First, there is no requirement to advance field-wide knowledge: the regulation states that a determination that research is undertaken for the purpose of discovering technological information "does not require the taxpayer be seeking to obtain information that exceeds, expands or refines the common knowledge of skilled professionals in the particular field of science or engineering in which the taxpayer is performing the research." Second, there is no requirement of technical or commercial success: the same paragraph provides that such a determination "does not require that the taxpayer succeed in developing a new or improved business component." Consistently, for contract research, Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(e)(2)(iii) treats research as performed on the taxpayer's behalf only if the agreement requires the taxpayer to bear the expense even if the research is not successful. Failed prototypes and abandoned engineering iterations are therefore creditable under IRC § 41, provided contemporaneous records show that the work was part of a process of experimentation aimed at resolving technical uncertainty.
3.2 The Compliance Shield: Six-Eye Review and TaxTrex Human-in-the-Loop Validation

items: A Qualified Engineer (Technical Eligibility Verification): Reviews primary engineering artifacts, such as system architecture diagrams, Git commit histories, CAD drawings, and test logs, and conducts technical interviews with the client's engineering leads (rather than only the chief financial officer) to confirm that the claimed activities relied on principles of the physical or biological sciences, engineering, or computer science and addressed genuine uncertainty about capability, method, or design under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(3)–(4).

A Scientist (Experimental Methodology Verification): Evaluates whether the project narrative and underlying iterative records (failed prototypes, laboratory notes, benchmark comparisons) demonstrate a systematic method of hypothesis, testing, analysis, and refinement sufficient to satisfy the 80% process-of-experimentation requirement of Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(5)–(6) and the standard applied in Siemer Milling, filtering out routine quality control and unstructured trial-and-error adjustments.

A CPA or Enrolled Agent (Financial and Legal Compliance Verification): Audits QRE tracing, wage inclusions and exclusions, base-period consistency under 26 U.S.C. § 41(c), controlled-group aggregation under § 41(f)(1), and third-party contract terms under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(e) and § 1.41-4A(d), to confirm that the research is not excluded as funded research under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(4)(H).

body.text: Section IV: Methodological Deep Dive: QRE Identification and Documentation Quality

Beyond compliance defense, dedicated R&D specialists can support larger legally defensible claims than ledger-only reviews by applying regulatory doctrines that require technical judgment, specifically project-level cost allocation, the shrinking-back rule, the 80% "substantially all" wage rule, and direct supervision and support tracing. Nothing in this section implies that any particular provider, including Pilot, fails to apply these doctrines; the comparison is between methods, not named firms.
4.1 Rigorous Cost Accounting and Project-Level Nexus

As confirmed by the RCCATG and the redesigned Form 6765 Section G (columns 49 and lines 50–56), taxpayers must establish a direct nexus linking accounting costs to specific business components. Systems that aggregate salaries by department (for example, pulling all payroll recorded under an "Engineering" cost center) fall short when cross-functional teams split their hours among qualified experimentation and non-qualified routine maintenance, debugging after the beginning of commercial production (excluded under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(4)(A)), or customer-specific adaptation (excluded under § 41(d)(4)(B)). Specialist consultancies typically establish project codes, time-tracking matrices, and engineering sprint mappings that disaggregate wages into direct conduct (Form 6765, line 50), direct supervision (line 51), and direct support (line 52) for each business component, which is precisely the data that Section G requires for tax years beginning after 2025.
4.2 Strategic Application of the "Shrinking-Back" Rule (Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(b)(2))

In substance, the regulation provides that the requirements of § 41(d) are applied first at the level of the discrete business component, meaning the product, process, computer software, technique, formula, or invention to be held for sale, lease, or license, or used in the taxpayer's trade or business. If the requirements are not met at that level, they are then applied at the level of the most significant subset of elements of the business component, and this "shrinking back" continues until either a subset of elements that satisfies the requirements is reached or the most basic element is reached and fails. The rule applies only if the overall business component does not satisfy the requirements, and the regulation expressly states that "[t]he shrinking-back rule is not itself applied as a reason to exclude research activities from credit eligibility."

To understand why ledger-only reviews can miss shrinking-back opportunities, consider a company that spends $1,000,000 upgrading an existing commercial software platform or manufacturing line, where 60% of the effort involves routine user-interface updates, standard API integrations, or off-the-shelf component assembly, and 40% involves developing a novel high-throughput data-ingestion algorithm or a custom mechanical subsystem. Evaluated at the level of the overall platform or machine, the project fails the Four-Part Test because only 40% of the research activities, less than the 80% "substantially all" threshold of Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(6), are elements of a process of experimentation. A superficial review either disqualifies the entire project (losing the credit entirely) or improperly claims the entire platform, creating an audit exposure of the kind seen in Little Sandy Coal, where the taxpayer's all-or-nothing claim for entire vessels prevented the courts from applying the shrinking-back rule. A specialist instead applies Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(b)(2) to shrink the business component down to the specific subsystem (the custom algorithm or mechanical subsystem). If 80% or more of the activities on that subset constitute a process of experimentation, the QREs attributable to the subset can be claimed and substantiated.
4.3 Complex QRE Identification: The Two 80% "Substantially All" Rules and Direct Supervision and Support

First, under the employee wage rule (26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2)(B); Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(d)(2)), when an employee performs both qualified and non-qualified services, generally only the wages allocable to qualified services are QREs under § 1.41-2(d)(1). However, if the wages allocated to qualified services (actual conduct, direct supervision, or direct support of qualified research) constitute at least 80% of the employee's wages for the taxable year, then all of the employee's services are treated as qualified services and 100% of that employee's wages for the year qualify. Second, under the process-of-experimentation rule (26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1)(C); Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(6)), applied separately to each business component and computed without regard to the § 1.41-2(d)(2) wage rule, at least 80% of the research activities on a business component, measured on a cost or other consistently applied reasonable basis, must be elements of a process of experimentation for the component to qualify. As the Seventh Circuit held in Little Sandy Coal, direct support and direct supervision activities are included in both the numerator and the denominator of that fraction.

Under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(c)(2) and (c)(3), qualified services also extend beyond employees with "engineer" or "R&D" job titles. Direct supervision (§ 1.41-2(c)(2)) means the immediate supervision (first-line management) of qualified research; it can include, for example, a vice president of engineering or chief technology officer who personally serves as the first-line manager of experimental architecture work, even if that person does not write code or run experiments, but it excludes higher-level managers to whom first-line managers report. Direct support (§ 1.41-2(c)(3)) means services in the direct support of persons engaged in the actual conduct of qualified research or persons directly supervising them, such as a machinist fabricating parts for an experimental prototype, a laboratory worker cleaning experimental equipment, or a clerk compiling test results, and it does not include general administrative services. By conducting functional interviews and corroborating actual time spent through calendars, sprint trackers, performance records, and commit logs, specialists can substantiate both the additional wages of core engineers who meet the 80% threshold and the qualified portion of first-line supervisors' and support staff's time.
4.4 Hypothetical Worked Example: Ledger-Only Capture vs. Specialist Methodology

To illustrate the arithmetic of these statutory and regulatory rules, consider a hypothetical worked example involving a U.S. software and hardware startup (a qualified small business under 26 U.S.C. § 41(h), with $1.8 million in current-year gross receipts and three years of operating history) developing an edge-computing device and software platform during its 2026 taxable year. The "ledger-only" column below represents a hypothetical review that relies on payroll and general ledger data without technical interviews; it is not a description of Pilot's documented workflow, which (as Section 2.1 explains) includes an interview and a written study. Pilot's 20% fee is applied only to show how a percentage fee interacts with the resulting credit.

items: Lead Systems Engineer wages and the 80% rule (Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(d)(2)): The startup pays a lead systems engineer $180,000 in wages. Time-tracking records show that the engineer spent 85% of annual hours directly conducting qualified research and 15% on administrative meetings. A basic allocation without the 80% rule yields $180,000 × 85% = $153,000. Because 85% is at least 80%, the specialist study qualifies 100% of the engineer's wages: $180,000 × 100% = $180,000, an additional $27,000 of QREs.

Chief technology officer first-line supervision (Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(c)(2)): The CTO earns $200,000 in wages. Because the title is an executive role, the ledger-only review excludes the CTO entirely ($0). Through functional interviews and sprint review logs, the specialist substantiates that the CTO spent 35% of working time as the immediate, first-line supervisor of the engineering experiments, capturing $200,000 × 35% = $70,000 (reported on Form 6765, Section G, line 51).

Shrinking-back subsystem capture (Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(b)(2)): Two software developers (combined wages of $240,000) work on the company's main commercial application. Overall, 60% of the work on the application is routine maintenance and interface styling, so the application fails the 80% process-of-experimentation threshold at the product level, yielding $0 in the ledger-only review. However, 50% of the developers' annual time was dedicated to building a discrete, novel data-compression subsystem on which 90% of the activities constituted systematic hypothesis testing. Shrinking back to that subsystem, the specialist qualifies $240,000 × 50% = $120,000 in direct-conduct wages (Form 6765, Section G, line 50).

Off-premises cloud computing (26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2)(A)(iii); Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(b)(4)): The company spends $50,000 on third-party cloud servers. The ledger-only review skips the mixed-use hosting account ($0), while the specialist separates staging and simulation environments from commercial production hosting and traces $20,000 to off-premises computer use in the conduct of qualified research, where the company is not the primary user of the provider's computers (Form 6765, Section G, line 55).

U.S. contract research (26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(3)(A); Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(e)): The startup pays $60,000 to an independent U.S. engineering contractor under a written agreement entered into before the work began, under which the startup retains substantial rights and bears the expense even if the research is unsuccessful. Both methods apply the statutory 65% limit: $60,000 × 65% = $39,000 (Form 6765, Section G, line 56).

Total QREs and Form 6765 Section B ASC computation (assuming no § 280C(c)(2) reduced-credit election): The ledger-only review totals $153,000 + $39,000 = $192,000 of QREs, while the specialist study totals $180,000 + $70,000 + $120,000 + $20,000 + $39,000 = $429,000 of QREs (Form 6765, line 48, carried to line 20). Under Scenario A (no QREs in at least one of the three prior years; 6% ASC rate), the ledger-only credit is $192,000 × 6% = $11,520.00 (or $9,216.00 net after a 20% fee of $2,304.00), and the specialist credit is $429,000 × 6% = $25,740.00 (before a fixed or hourly professional fee). Under Scenario B (an established claimant with $600,000 of total QREs over the prior three years; 14% ASC rate), the ASC base on line 22 is line 21 divided by 6.0 (equivalent to 50% of the three-year average): $600,000 ÷ 6.0 = $100,000.00. The ledger-only excess QREs are $192,000 − $100,000 = $92,000, producing a credit of $92,000 × 14% = $12,880.00 (or $10,304.00 net after a 20% fee of $2,576.00). The specialist excess QREs are $429,000 − $100,000 = $329,000, producing a credit of $329,000 × 14% = $46,060.00 (before a fixed or hourly professional fee).

body.text: Two cautions accompany this example. First, because the company in this example is a qualified small business, it could elect on Form 6765, Section D, to apply some or all of the credit against payroll taxes, but only on its timely filed original return. Second, if the company deducts its domestic research expenditures under § 174A and does not elect the reduced credit under § 280C(c)(2), § 280C(c)(1) reduces the § 174A amount by the full amount of the credit; if it elects the reduced credit, the Scenario A and Scenario B credits shown above are multiplied by 79% on Form 6765, line 26.

body.text: Section V: Risk Management and Audit Defense in the R&D Landscape
5.1 Analyzing Common Audit Triggers and IRS Enforcement

Pilot.com's own R&D materials state that the R&D tax credit program appears on the IRS's "Dirty Dozen" list of tax scams and that, after an audit, the IRS can review claims for up to seven years prior. Pilot does not cite a source for either statement on its product page. As a matter of federal law, the general assessment period is three years after a return is filed (26 U.S.C. § 6501(a)), and the general refund-claim period is the later of three years from filing or two years from payment (26 U.S.C. § 6511(a)); however, because unused research credits carry forward for up to 20 years under 26 U.S.C. § 39, the IRS may examine the computation of a credit generated in an earlier, closed year when that credit is used in an open year. Pilot's "seven years" figure should therefore be understood as a simplification rather than a statutory rule. Pilot's blog also asserts that "20% to 30% of all R&D claims [are] audited each year"; because Pilot cites no IRS data book or Statistics of Income source for that audit rate, it is recorded here as a vendor claim.

When an examination begins under the RCCATG, examiners use the guide's research credit claim checklist (Exhibit A) and mandatory research credit claim IDR (Exhibit C). The RCCATG addresses compliance with Notice 2008-39 (filing requirements for corporate research credit claims), whether a reduced-credit election under former § 280C(c)(3) (now § 280C(c)(2)) was validly made on a timely original return, review of the taxpayer's transcripts across credit-generation and carryover years, and potential penalties, including the 20% penalty for erroneous claims for refund or credit under 26 U.S.C. § 6676 and preparer penalties under 26 U.S.C. §§ 6694 and 6701 (which the RCCATG discusses in connection with invalid § 280C elections). The 20% accuracy-related penalty under 26 U.S.C. § 6662 may also apply to underpayments attributable to disallowed credits, as it did in Little Sandy Coal, although the RCCATG refers to accuracy-related penalties only in passing. Claims built on unverified software defaults or lacking project-level evidence of experimentation, as illustrated in Siemer Milling Co. v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2019-37, and Little Sandy Coal Co. v. Commissioner, 62 F.4th 287 (7th Cir. 2023), are particularly vulnerable once examiners request substantiation.
5.2 The Synthesis of Technology and Expertise: TaxTrex, Six-Eye Review, and creditARMOR

As described by the vendor, its free four-step mock-audit workflow allows companies and CPAs to (1) upload Form 6765 (with automatic parsing of Section G business components where completed); (2) upload project evidence across 11 documentary categories (such as payroll records, time allocations, technical specifications, test logs, contracts and statements of work, and calculations); (3) generate draft IDR-style examiner questions and short per-project responses, which the vendor says are cross-checked by multiple AI models and rated as strong, weak, or missing; and (4) receive a prioritized risk report and audit-readiness score before an IRS examiner reviews the file. These platform features are reported as vendor descriptions and were not independently tested for this edition.

Readers should therefore treat creditARMOR as a preparation and risk-assessment tool, not as an insurance policy, and should review the written engagement terms before relying on any audit-defense commitment.
Conclusions and Strategic Recommendations

items: Pilot.com's R&D credit offering is human-assisted, not purely automated, but it carries a 20% percentage-of-credit fee and sits within a generalist accounting practice. However, Pilot charges 20% of the total credit received (which would equal $100,000 on a $500,000 payroll credit), and live customer reviews on G2 (4.7/5.0 across 143 reviews) and Trustpilot (2.9/5.0 across 20 reviews) contain no Trustpilot discussion of R&D credits, while three 1-star Trustpilot reviewers criticize Pilot's tax services for pricing, communication, and the scope of work delivered.

Qualitative substantiation and the Form 6765 Section G requirement call for engineering-level rigor. With the Tax Court's full disallowance in Siemer Milling Co. v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2019-37, the Seventh Circuit's rejection of arbitrary time allocations and all-or-nothing claims in Little Sandy Coal Co. v. Commissioner, 62 F.4th 287 (7th Cir. 2023), the end of the IRS's refund-claim perfection transition period on January 10, 2026, and the shift of Form 6765 Section G from optional (tax years beginning before 2026) to required (tax years beginning after 2025) subject to limited exceptions, taxpayers must document project-level hypotheses, systematic experimentation, and component-level wage, supply, computer, and contract research costs contemporaneously.

Dedicated specialists can support larger defensible claims through careful application of regulatory doctrines and non-contingent multidisciplinary review, but their own marketing claims require the same scrutiny. By publishing fixed-fee and hourly pricing ($195–$395 per hour) rather than percentage-of-credit fees, and by committing to a mandatory Six-Eye Review (engineer, scientist, and CPA or enrolled agent) and creditARMOR mock-audit testing, the specialist model aims to reduce fee-related conflicts and to align front-end documentation with IRS examination standards.
